pages.heading: Concepts of IoT
pages.summary: Concepts of IoT 6042A full-screen Kerala Polytechnic handbook.
pages.content: 6042A Concepts of IoT Corrected lesson path for Course Code 6042A . This handbook explains IoT fundamentals, M2M, architecture, sensors, actuators, Arduino, NodeMCU, Raspberry Pi, communication protocols, cloud connectivity and domain applications. Course overview IoT means connecting physical things to digital systems using sensors, controllers, communication networks, cloud platforms and applications. The core engineering question is simple: what data must be sensed, how it is processed, where it is transmitted, and what action must happen. Module 1 - IoT fundamentals Definition Internet of Things is a network of physical objects embedded with sensors, electronics, software and connectivity so that they can collect, exchange and act on data. IoT vs M2M M2M is machine-to-machine communication, often point-to-point. IoT is broader and usually includes internet/cloud integration, analytics, dashboards and scalable device management. Basic architecture Device layer → connectivity layer → data processing/cloud layer → application layer. Security, power management and maintenance are required across all layers. Module 2 - IoT hardware platforms Arduino Good for simple sensor reading, digital/analog I/O and actuator control. It is easy for beginner embedded experiments. NodeMCU / ESP8266 Microcontroller board with Wi-Fi. Suitable for low-cost network-connected sensor nodes and control projects. Raspberry Pi Single-board computer running Linux. Suitable when camera, database, web server or heavier processing is needed. Sensors and actuators Sensors convert physical quantities into electrical data. Actuators convert control signals into action, such as relay switching, motor movement or indication. Module 3 - Communication and protocols Wi-Fi Common for internet access where power and network coverage are available. Bluetooth Used for short-range personal/device communication. MQTT Lightweight publish/subscribe protocol. It uses broker, publisher, subscriber and topic. HTTP Request/response protocol used for web APIs and dashboards. Data flow example Temperature sensor reads machine room temperature → NodeMCU sends value by MQTT → cloud dashboard displays trend → alert is generated if the value crosses limit. Module 4 - Applications and engineering use Smart home Lighting, security, energy monitoring and appliance control. Industry Condition monitoring, predictive maintenance, production tracking and alarms. Healthcare Wearables, remote monitoring and equipment status logging. Escalator/electrical relevance IoT can monitor controller status, temperature, energy use, run hours and fault alarms, but safety-critical control must follow approved industrial standards. Question bank Define IoT and explain its architecture. Compare IoT and M2M communication. Explain sensors and actuators used in IoT. Compare Arduino, NodeMCU and Raspberry Pi. Explain MQTT with publisher, broker, subscriber and topic. Explain IoT applications in industry. Describe security challenges in IoT. Design a basic IoT temperature monitoring system. Model question paper Quick facts Do not merge: 6042A is not 6042. Filename: lessons-6042A.html Main idea: sense → process → communicate → act.

pages.title: Contemporary Electronics 6042B | Kerala Polytechnic Handbook
pages.heading: Contemporary Electronics
pages.summary: Contemporary Electronics 6042B complete Kerala Polytechnic handbook covering consumer electronics, entertainment systems, home appliances, backup power, batteries, electric vehicles and charging standards.
pages.content: Handbook Navigator Contemporary Electronics A full-screen handbook for Course Code 6042B . This guide converts the syllabus into a complete learning document covering daily-life electronics, entertainment devices, domestic appliances, backup systems, batteries, electric vehicles, charging methods, connectors, standards, calculations, diagrams, revision points and model answers. ഈ വിഷയത്തിൽ theory മാത്രം പോരാ. ഓരോ device-നും construction, working principle, block diagram, specification, maintenance, application എന്നിവ ചേർത്ത് പഠിച്ചാൽ answer strong ആകും. Official Course Structure The syllabus objective is to provide knowledge-level information about electronic devices used in everyday life. The course has four outcomes: applications of electronics, entertainment devices, domestic appliances and power backup, and EV charging standards. How to write answers Start with definition or purpose. Draw a neat block diagram or simple schematic. Explain each block in the signal/power flow order. Add specifications, advantages, limitations and applications. Finish with maintenance/safety if the device is appliance, UPS, battery or EV charger. Engineering connection For an electronics technician, this subject is practical: panel displays, SMPS, UPS backup, sensors, motor-driven appliances, display interfaces and EV charging are common field-service areas. Block diagram മനസ്സിലാക്കിയാൽ fault finding എളുപ്പമാകും. Power path, signal path, control path വേർതിരിച്ച് കാണുക. Consumer Electronics Fundamentals History of electronic devices, vacuum tubes, transistors, integrated circuits, Moore's Law, microprocessors, microcontrollers and their use in consumer electronics. Evolution of electronic devices Vacuum tube → transistor → IC → microprocessor → microcontroller എന്നതാണ് basic development path. Moore's Law Moore's Law is the observation that transistor count in ICs tends to increase rapidly with technology advancement. In consumer electronics it results in smaller, faster, cheaper and more power-efficient products. Microprocessor vs Microcontroller Microprocessor: CPU only; used where high processing is needed. Microcontroller: CPU, memory, I/O and peripherals on one chip. Microcontroller is preferred in washing machine, remote, AC, microwave and toys because cost and power are low. Consumer controller blocks Sensor/input → microcontroller → display/actuator is the most common control pattern in consumer electronics. Input: button, remote, sensor. Processing: firmware and timing logic. Output: display, buzzer, relay, motor driver. Applications TV and set-top box decoding and display control. Washing machine sequence and motor control. Microwave timer, keypad, display and magnetron control. AC temperature and compressor control. UPS battery monitoring and switching. Entertainment Electronics Systems Microphones, loudspeakers, AM/FM receivers, stereo, 2.1/5.1 home theatre, display systems, video resolution, ports and video players. Audio entertainment chain Microphone converts sound into electrical signal. Pre-amplifier raises weak signal level. Tone or digital processor shapes audio quality. Power amplifier supplies enough power. Loudspeaker converts electrical signal back to sound. Microphone and loudspeaker AM and FM receiver Antenna receives radio frequency signal. Tuner selects the required station frequency. RF/IF stages amplify and filter the selected signal. Detector/demodulator extracts audio. Audio amplifier drives the loudspeaker. Radio receiver-ൽ antenna signal എടുക്കുന്നു, tuner station select ചെയ്യുന്നു, demodulator audio വേർതിരിക്കുന്നു. Display parameters Ports and connectors VGA Analog video port used in older monitors/projectors. Video only. Composite AV Yellow RCA for video and red/white for audio. Simple but lower quality. S-Video Separates brightness and colour information. Better than composite but mostly obsolete. HDMI Digital audio and video through one cable. Supports HD and 4K depending version. Optical port Uses light through fibre for digital audio and avoids electrical noise. DVD / Blu-ray Blu-ray supports higher storage and video quality than DVD. Home Appliances, Solar, UPS and Batteries Working principle of domestic appliances and power backup systems: washing machines, microwave oven, induction stove, air conditioners, solar systems, UPS/inverter and storage batteries. Washing machine User selects program using control panel. Controller checks door lock and water level sensor. Inlet valve fills water; motor rotates drum/agitator. Drain pump removes water. Spin cycle removes moisture using high-speed rotation. Important parts: drum, motor, inlet valve, drain pump, pressure sensor, door lock and control board. Microwave oven and induction stove Microwave water molecule heating ഉപയോഗിക്കുന്നു. Induction stove vessel-ൽ eddy current heating ഉണ്ടാക്കുന്നു. Air conditioner basics AC removes indoor heat using vapour compression refrigeration. Main parts: compressor, condenser, expansion device, evaporator, fan, refrigerant and control board. Non-inverter AC: compressor switches ON/OFF at fixed speed. Inverter AC: compressor speed varies according to load; better comfort and energy saving. 1 ton AC: approximately 12000 BTU/hour cooling capacity. Solar power system On-grid: connected to utility grid and usually works without battery. Off-grid: independent system requiring battery backup. PV panel converts sunlight into DC. Charge controller regulates charging. Battery stores energy in off-grid system. Inverter converts DC to AC for loads. UPS and inverter Offline UPS: load normally on mains; switches to battery inverter during failure. Online UPS: load continuously supplied through inverter; no transfer delay. Line-interactive UPS: includes voltage regulation and battery backup. Inverter: converts DC battery supply to AC for longer backup. Storage batteries Electric Vehicle and Charging Standards EV schematic, charging equipment, slow/fast chargers, AC/DC charging, EVSE modes, charging

pages.title: Introduction to Hybrid and Electric Vehicles 6042C | Polytechnic Handbook
pages.heading: Introduction to Hybrid and Electric Vehicles
pages.summary: 6042C Introduction to Hybrid and Electric Vehicles full-screen handbook for Kerala Polytechnic open elective. Covers EV basics, vehicle dynamics, drive trains, motors, batteries, sizing, CAN, energy management and charging stations.
pages.content: Handbook Index Do not study this like a story. For every topic, draw the block diagram, write power flow, then write application. Introduction to Hybrid and Electric Vehicles A full-screen handbook for course code 6042C . It converts the official syllabus into a usable study guide with concepts, diagrams, equations, solved examples, quick revision, Malayalam support notes and exam practice. This is structured as a handbook for understanding EV systems from vehicle motion to charging station level. EV System View Syllabus Structure Converted to Study Plan The subject has four outcomes: EV and HEV technologies, energy efficiency of drive trains, power and energy need of EV/HEV, and energy management strategies. The handbook follows the same order so exam preparation stays aligned. Course Objectives Design and develop basic schemes of electric and hybrid electric vehicles. Choose suitable drive scheme based on application and resources. Understand EV motors, batteries, charging, smart charging and EV trends. EV എന്നത് battery മാത്രം അല്ല. Battery, converter, motor, mechanical load, controller, CAN communication, charging station എന്നിവ ചേർന്ന complete system ആണ്. CO and Hour Distribution Module Roadmap Module 1 — EV and Hybrid Vehicle Foundation Need, history, principle of operation, EV types, vehicle motion equations, forces, social and environmental importance. Need for Electric Vehicles Transportation consumes large fuel energy and creates urban emissions. EVs reduce tail-pipe emissions, allow regenerative braking, use efficient electric motors and can use renewable-grid energy. The real benefit depends on electricity source, battery life, charging infrastructure and recycling. EV Types BEV: Battery electric vehicle, no ICE propulsion. HEV: ICE and electric machine share propulsion and energy recovery. PHEV: HEV with larger battery and external charging. FCEV: Fuel cell produces electricity from hydrogen. Solar vehicle: Solar panels assist charging; practical power is limited by area and sunlight. Hybrid Vehicle Meaning A hybrid vehicle uses at least two energy sources or converters. Normal HEV uses chemical fuel through ICE and electrochemical battery through motor. Hybridization allows engine stop-start, regenerative braking, peak torque assist and efficient operating-point control. Social and Economic Importance EVs reduce local pollution, reduce oil dependence, create battery/charging industries and support renewable energy integration. Challenges include high initial cost, battery raw materials, range anxiety, recycling and charging infrastructure. Vehicle Dynamic Equations The traction motor must overcome road-load forces. In design problems, first calculate force, then power, then motor/battery requirement. Mini Solved Example Problem: A 1000 kg EV travels at 20 m/s on level road. Crr = 0.015, ρ = 1.2 kg/m³, Cd = 0.30, frontal area = 2.2 m². Acceleration is zero. Find wheel power. Rolling force = 0.015 × 1000 × 9.81 = 147.15 N. Aero drag = 0.5 × 1.2 × 0.30 × 2.2 × 20² = 158.4 N. Total force = 305.55 N. Power = 305.55 × 20 = 6111 W ≈ 6.1 kW. Module 2 — Electric Drive Trains and Propulsion Units Electric traction, drive-train topologies, power flow control, efficiency analysis, electric propulsion components and motor-drive comparison. Electric Drive Train Blocks Energy source: battery, fuel cell or supercapacitor. Power converter: DC-DC converter, inverter and charger. Traction motor: DC motor, induction motor, PMSM/BLDC or SRM. Transmission: fixed gear, differential or wheel drive. Control system: accelerator input, motor controller, BMS, protection and communication. Power Flow Modes Motor Drive Comparison Hybrid Drive-Train Topologies Series Hybrid ICE drives generator; generator supplies motor/battery; wheels are driven only by motor. Mechanically simple, but multiple energy conversions create loss. Parallel Hybrid ICE and motor can both drive wheels. Efficient for highway operation, but mechanical coupling is more complex. Series-Parallel Hybrid Combines series and parallel benefits using power-split mechanism. Control is advanced but energy optimization is better. Plug-in Hybrid Large battery can be externally charged. It gives electric-only range and ICE backup for long trips. Hybrid topology answer എഴുതുമ്പോൾ source → converter → motor → wheel power flow arrow must be clear. Efficiency Chain If battery efficiency is 0.95, inverter efficiency 0.96, motor efficiency 0.92 and gear efficiency 0.97, overall efficiency = 0.95 × 0.96 × 0.92 × 0.97 = 0.814 ≈ 81.4%. Module 3 — Energy Storage and Drive System Sizing Battery parameters, chemistry comparison, fuel cells, supercapacitors, flywheel, hybrid storage and rating calculation. Battery Parameters Voltage: decides inverter and motor drive level. Capacity Ah: amount of charge available. Energy Wh: voltage × Ah. SOC: remaining battery percentage. SOH: ageing condition. C-rate: charge/discharge rate relative to capacity. Specific energy: Wh/kg, important for range. Specific power: W/kg, important for acceleration. Storage Comparison Drive Sizing Method Fix vehicle mass, speed, acceleration, gradient and range target. Calculate rolling, aerodynamic, gradient and acceleration forces. Calculate wheel power and motor shaft power after drivetrain loss. Select motor peak power and continuous power. Select inverter current, voltage and thermal rating. Calculate battery energy from range and Wh/km consumption. Add reserve for ageing, temperature, depth of discharge and safety margin. Key Sizing Equations Mini Solved Example — Battery Pack Capacity Problem: An EV consumes 120 Wh/km and must travel 80 km. Pack voltage is 300 V. Assume usable depth is 80%. Find required nominal battery capacity. Usable energy required = 120 × 80 = 9600 Wh. Nominal energy = 9600 / 0.8 = 12000 Wh. Capacity Ah = 12000 / 300 = 40 Ah. Answer: A 300 V, 40 Ah pack is the minimum nominal capacity before adding design margin. Module 4 — Communication, Energy Managemen

pages.title: Introduction to Multimedia 6042D | Kerala Polytechnic Handbook
pages.heading: Introduction to Multimedia
pages.summary: Introduction to Multimedia 6042D full-screen Kerala Polytechnic handbook.
pages.content: 6042D Introduction to Multimedia Corrected lesson path for Course Code 6042D . This handbook covers multimedia components, project stages, text, hypertext, digital audio, MIDI, compression, images, colour, video, animation and multimedia networks. Course overview Multimedia is not just presentation design. It is the engineering of different media objects so that they can be created, stored, compressed, transmitted, synchronized and delivered to users. Module 1 - Multimedia basics and project stages Definition Multimedia is the integrated use of text, graphics, image, animation, audio and video under computer control. Interactive multimedia lets the user control navigation. Components Text, graphics, images, audio, video, animation and interactivity. Each component must be selected based on purpose, quality and delivery platform. Digital transition Digital media allows editing, compression, search, copying, storage, networking, indexing and interaction compared with conventional fixed media. Project stages Requirement → planning → storyboard → content creation → authoring → testing → delivery → maintenance. Tools Input devices include camera, microphone and scanner. Production tools include image editor, audio editor, video editor, animation software, presentation tools and authoring systems. Module 2 - Text, audio and compression Text and fonts Text provides headings, navigation, captions, instructions and accessibility. Bitmap fonts are pixel based. Outline fonts are curve based and scalable. Unicode supports international character sets. Hypertext Hypertext is linked text. Hypermedia extends links to image, audio, video and animation. Node is an information unit; anchor is the clickable source; link connects nodes. Digital audio Digital audio is created by sampling and quantizing an analog sound wave. Important terms: frequency, bandwidth, decibel, sampling rate, bit depth and channels. MIDI MIDI stores musical instructions, not actual waveform. It is small and useful for synthesized music. Digitized audio stores actual sound samples. Compression methods Lossless compression recovers original data exactly. Lossy compression removes less noticeable information. Methods include RLE, Huffman coding, dictionary coding, arithmetic coding, sliding window compression and silence compression. Module 3 - Image fundamentals Image basics A digital image is a 2D array of pixels. Quality depends on resolution, colour depth, dynamic range, display and compression. Colour RGB is used for displays, CMYK for printing, HSV/HSL for colour selection and grayscale for intensity-only images. Palette means limited colour table. Dithering simulates unavailable colours with patterns. Formats JPEG idea JPEG divides the image into blocks, applies transform coding, quantizes details and entropy-codes the result. It is lossy and suitable for photos, not sharp text diagrams. Module 4 - Video, animation and networks Video basics Video is a sequence of frames. Important terms: frame rate, resolution, aspect ratio, bitrate, codec and container. Compression Video compression removes spatial redundancy within frames and temporal redundancy between frames. Motion compensation stores movement and differences instead of every full frame. Animation Cell animation uses frame-by-frame drawings. Computer animation uses keyframes and interpolation. Morphing transforms one image/object into another. Networks Multimedia networks require bandwidth, low delay, low jitter, low packet loss, buffering and synchronization. Applications include multimedia over IP, ATM, conferencing and media-on-demand. Formula and file bank Format logic: photo - JPEG, diagram - PNG, animation icon - GIF, archive scan - TIFF, audio edit - WAV, compressed music - MP3/AAC, music instructions - MIDI, common video - MP4. Question bank Define multimedia and explain its components. Explain transition from conventional media to digital media. Explain stages of a multimedia project. Compare bitmap and outline fonts. Define hypertext, hypermedia, node, anchor and link. Explain audio digitization and data rate. Compare MIDI and digitized audio. Explain lossless and lossy compression with examples. Explain colour models, palette and dithering. Compare GIF, JPEG, PNG and TIFF. Explain motion compensation in video compression. Explain multimedia over IP and media-on-demand. Model paper Quick facts Do not merge: 6042D is not 6042. Filename: lessons-6042D.html Heavy module: Module 2 has 20 hours.

pages.summary: Complete Kerala Polytechnic Revision 2021 handbook for Course 6043 VLSI and DSP Fundamentals: materials, construction practices, foundations, openings and roofs with Malayalam support, diagrams, questions and printable notes.
pages.content: Course 6043 VLSI and DSP Fundamentals A complete diploma handbook for Course 6043. It turns the supplied official syllabus into a practical learning and exam-preparation resource for all modules, learning supports, and exam preparation materials as per the official syllabus. Materials become buildings only through informed construction practice. A good civil technician connects material properties with location, exposure, workmanship, inspection and maintenance. The course moves from stone and brick to foundation, openings and roofs. Official source declaration and course dashboard Course facts, module coverage, activities and assessment data below are transcribed from the supplied official course PDF. Teaching explanations, diagrams, practice questions and model paper are POLY PMNA study support, not an official examination paper. Source-integrity note The user confirmed this source for placement in the Revision 2021 lesson library. However, each supplied PDF page footer reads “Diploma Curriculum Revision 2026”. This handbook therefore uses Revision 2021 for the website label and file location as instructed, while preserving the discrepancy transparently. Students must confirm their active curriculum scheme with their institution or SITTTR before relying on a syllabus for examination decisions. Confirmed course facts Course objectives Understand classification, properties, manufacture, testing and suitability of stone, timber, lime, bricks, blocks and alternative materials. Identify finishing materials, wood products, glass, metals, special materials, industrial/agro waste products and structural steel sections. Become familiar with prefabrication, site layout, earthwork and foundation practices. Understand the types, components, fittings and functional requirements of openings, roofs, trusses and vertical communication systems. Course outcomes CO–PO mapping Legend: 1 = low correlation, 2 = medium correlation and 3 = high correlation. The PDF totals are PO1 = 12 and PO2 = 6. Syllabus roadmap Use the hours as a guide for study effort. A short module is not a reason to skip its drawing, selection logic or common mistakes. M1 study route Classify materials and make sound first-stage choices for stone, timber, lime, bricks, blocks and alternative masonry units. Classify natural, artificial, special, finished and recycled materials. Recognise properties that make a material suitable for a construction duty. Connect raw material, manufacture, test and field use. M2 study route Select surface, board, glass, metal, insulating and special materials by service condition rather than appearance alone. Compare flooring and finish options for function, wear and maintenance. Identify common wood products, glass and metal uses. Recognise insulating, waste-derived and special processed materials. M3 study route Move from material knowledge to the organised construction of a safe substructure, including layout, excavation and foundation choice. Explain prefabrication and basic structural-steel building methods. Follow the logical sequence from site clearance to setting out and excavation. Choose a foundation concept from ground and loading conditions. M4 study route Understand building openings, movement systems and roofs as functional assemblies that must control access, light, air, water and load. Identify common doors, windows, ventilators and their functions. Explain stairs, lifts and escalators at an introductory building-components level. Compare flat and pitched roofs and recognise roof-truss terminology. Basic building materials Classify materials and make sound first-stage choices for stone, timber, lime, bricks, blocks and alternative masonry units. Learning goals Classify natural, artificial, special, finished and recycled materials. Recognise properties that make a material suitable for a construction duty. Connect raw material, manufacture, test and field use. Engineering habit Observe the service condition first. Then identify material or component properties, construction detail, inspection point, safety condition and maintenance consequence. Exam habit Start with the official term, define it clearly, classify or list the required points, use a labelled sketch where useful, and conclude with a relevant construction application. M1.1 — Classification of materials Classification of materials Official syllabus focus: Types: natural, artificial, special, finished and recycled. Classify a material first by origin and then by performance. Natural materials such as stone and timber need selection and processing; artificial materials such as bricks and blocks are manufactured to a controlled form. Finished or special products are selected for a particular function such as protection, appearance or strength. When comparing options for a wall, record the source, expected exposure, weight, durability and availability before choosing it. Material classification tells a site team what inspection, storage and workmanship controls may be required. Before approving or explaining this item, identify the service condition, expected load or exposure, workmanship requirement, inspection point and likely consequence of a poor choice. Do not select a material or construction method from appearance alone. Relate the decision to moisture, load, durability, detail, safety and maintenance. M1.2 — Stone Stone Official syllabus focus: Classification of rocks: igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic. Rock origin affects texture, structure and likely behaviour. Igneous rocks form from cooling molten material, sedimentary rocks form from deposited layers, and metamorphic rocks are altered by heat and pressure. A civil technician should not assume that every hard-looking stone has equal resistance to water, weathering or load. Observe bedding, grain, cracks and water absorption before accepting stone for a structural or facing purpose. Correct rock identification supports appropriate use in foundations, masonry, aggregates

pages.title: 1001 — English for Technical Communication | Polytechnic Handbook
pages.heading: English for Technical Communication
pages.summary: Complete handbook lesson for Course 1001 — English for Technical Communication
pages.content: English for Technical Communication A complete study handbook for listening, speaking, reading, writing, language accuracy, translation, AI-supported communication, and professional expression. This handbook expands every official module and detailed-syllabus row in the supplied SITTTR source into a student-friendly learning path. Technical terms remain in English; Malayalam support notes are provided separately to clarify difficult ideas. How this handbook was prepared The verified extracted text for Course Code 1001 was used as the authoritative source for course information, objectives, course outcomes, CO–PO mapping, modules, major topics, detailed syllabus, activities, assessment structures, learning resources, equipment requirements, and references. Educational explanations, examples, Malayalam support, and study guidance are handbook elaborations. They are not claimed to be verbatim statements from the official PDF. At a glance How to use this handbook 1. Learn Read the concept explanation and the Malayalam support note. Keep the standard English term beside its meaning. 2. Practise Attempt the guided examples, activities, short-answer questions, and writing tasks without copying the model answer. 3. Perform Use the assessment section to rehearse listening, reading, speaking, writing, translation, AI-tool use, and practical-test performance. What the course expects Course objectives Develop the ability to listen effectively and comprehend a wide range of information, viewpoints, and ideas in formal and informal contexts. Enhance proficiency, fluency, and confidence in spoken English for academic, workplace, and everyday situations. Use effective reading strategies to understand and evaluate technical and non-technical texts. Produce accurate, concise, and clear writing across technical, professional, and creative forms of discourse. Course outcomes CO–PO matrix Legend from source: 1 = Low, 2 = Medium, 3 = High, and “–” = No Correlation. Every official syllabus item is represented Major-topic coverage Module I: 3 major-topic rows. Module II: 2 major-topic rows. Module III: 6 major-topic rows. Module IV: 3 major-topic rows. Detailed-syllabus coverage Module I: 5 detailed rows. Module II: 5 detailed rows. Module III: 6 detailed rows. Module IV: 3 detailed rows. Prose This module develops comprehension, summary writing, vocabulary building, sentence accuracy, and language use in real-life situations. 1. Listening/Reading and comprehending a technology-related inspirational speech or story Concept Comprehension means constructing meaning from spoken or written language. In a technology-related speech or story, the learner should identify the central message, the situation, the speaker’s purpose, important facts, sequence, and supporting details. Listening and reading use different physical channels, but both require attention, prediction, selection of evidence, and checking of meaning. Method Preview the title and predict the subject. Listen or read once for the main idea without stopping for every unfamiliar word. Read or listen again and record the five questions: who, what, when, where, and why. Separate the central message from examples, illustrations, and repeated phrases. Answer in complete sentences and support answers with details from the passage. 2. Summarising a passage A summary is a shorter form of a passage that retains its essential meaning. It should be objective, coherent, and written in the learner’s own words. A summary is not a collection of copied sentences and not a personal opinion. Summary procedure Read for overall meaning. Underline the central idea and essential points. Remove examples, repetition, minor descriptions, and personal comments. Group related points and arrange them logically. Write a concise paragraph and check grammar. Quality checklist Meaning is preserved. Important cause-and-effect links remain. Pronouns and tense are consistent. No new claim is introduced. Length is appropriate to the task. Word-count calculator for summary practice 3. Word formation — prefixes, suffixes, synonyms, antonyms, and homonyms Word formation helps a learner infer meaning and select accurate vocabulary. A prefix is added before a base word, while a suffix is added after it. Synonyms have similar meanings, antonyms show contrast, and homonyms have the same spelling or pronunciation but different meanings. Engineering-context method When an unfamiliar word appears in a technical passage, identify the base word, examine nearby prefixes or suffixes, use the sentence context, and test whether the inferred word fits the grammar. Do not assume that a familiar-looking word has the same meaning in every technical context. 4. Structure of a sentence, articles, auxiliaries, and concord Sentence structure A sentence normally expresses a complete thought. A useful basic pattern is Subject + Verb + Object/Complement . Longer sentences may add time, place, manner, condition, or reason. Clauses must be connected with suitable conjunctions and punctuation. Articles Use a before a singular countable noun beginning with a consonant sound, an before a singular countable noun beginning with a vowel sound, and the when the listener or reader can identify the specific noun. Some plural and uncountable nouns take no article when used generally. Auxiliary verbs Primary auxiliaries be, have, do support tense, questions, negatives, and passive construction. Modal auxiliaries such as can, may, must, should express ability, possibility, obligation, or advice. The main verb form must agree with the auxiliary. Concord Subject–verb agreement means that the verb form matches the subject in number and person: “The instrument works” but “The instruments work.” Intervening phrases must not distract the writer from the true subject. 5. Situational English Situational English means choosing language according to the purpose, relationship, place, and level of formality. A workplace request should be cle

pages.title: 1002 — Fundamentals of Engineering Mathematics
pages.heading: Fundamentals of Engineering Mathematics
pages.summary: Complete Polytechnic handbook for 1002 — Fundamentals of Engineering Mathematics
pages.content: Fundamentals of Engineering Mathematics Course 1002 · Semester I · Theory · 60 contact hours · 4 credits This handbook develops the four mathematical toolsets specified in the syllabus: matrices and determinants, trigonometry, coordinate geometry, and differential calculus. How the source was used The verified SITTTR syllabus text was treated as authoritative for course information, objectives, outcomes, CO–PO mapping, modules, detailed topics, instructional hours, activities, assessment, requirements, and references. How this handbook is organised This course introduces fundamental mathematical tools used in engineering. It includes Matrices and Determinants, Trigonometry, Coordinate Geometry, and Differential Calculus, which help students understand and solve engineering and real-life problems. How to use this handbook 1. Learn Read the concept explanation, then restate it in your own words without changing technical terms, symbols, or units. 2. Practise Attempt the worked example and the linked activity. For drawing/CAD courses, reproduce the sequence with instruments or software. 3. Recall Close the topic, answer the module questions, and use the formula bank and revision checklist. Objectives, COs and programme mapping Official course objectives To introduce the basic concepts of Matrices and Determinants and their applications in solving system of linear equations. To develop a comprehensive understanding of trigonometric concepts and to analyze trigonometric relationships. To familiarize with Coordinate Geometry for representing and studying some basic concepts of straight lines and circles. To provide fundamental knowledge of Differential Calculus. Course outcomes CO–PO matrix Complete syllabus coverage checklist Every official major topic and detailed-syllabus entry is represented in the module sections. Use the checklist for deliberate study rather than skipping a difficult topic. Matrices and Determinants Matrices provide a compact language for simultaneous relationships and engineering data. This module builds the algebra needed to solve two- and three-unknown systems. Learning goals Classify matrices and identify order. Perform transpose and matrix operations. Evaluate determinants and use Cramer’s rule. Find minors, cofactors, adjoint and inverse. Key facts Order is written rows × columns. Matrix multiplication is row-by-column. An inverse exists only when the determinant is non-zero. Cramer’s rule replaces columns with constants. Basic concept of a matrix and special types of matrices A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of quantities written in rows and columns. Its order is m × n when it has m rows and n columns. Recognise row, column, square, diagonal, triangular, identity and zero matrices before performing operations. The position of an entry is identified by its row and column indices. A square matrix has equal numbers of rows and columns; an identity matrix has ones on the principal diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Transpose of a matrix The transpose changes rows into columns. If A = [aᵢⱼ], then Aᵀ = [aⱼᵢ]. The order m × n becomes n × m. Important properties include (Aᵀ)ᵀ = A and (A + B)ᵀ = Aᵀ + Bᵀ. Carefully copy the main diagonal and reflect entries across it. Algebra of matrices: scalar multiplication, equality, addition, subtraction and multiplication Equality requires equal order and equal corresponding entries. Addition and subtraction are possible only for matrices of the same order. Scalar multiplication multiplies every entry by the scalar. Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative: AB may exist while BA does not, or AB ≠ BA. Use row-by-column multiplication and retain the correct order. Determinants and Cramer’s rule for two and three unknowns The determinant is a scalar associated with a square matrix. For a second-order matrix, det(A)=ad−bc. For a third-order determinant, expand by a row or column using signed cofactors. Cramer’s rule replaces one column of the coefficient determinant with the constants. It is valid when the coefficient determinant is non-zero. Apply the same idea to three unknowns by forming Δ, Δₓ, Δᵧ and Δ_z. Minors, cofactors, adjoint and inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix The minor Mᵢⱼ is the determinant obtained after deleting row i and column j. The cofactor is Cᵢⱼ = (−1)ⁱ⁺ʲMᵢⱼ. The adjoint is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. To solve AX=B using an inverse, calculate X=A⁻¹B. If |A|=0, the inverse does not exist. Problems and engineering applications Problems consolidate all matrix operations. A safe solution sequence is: write the data as matrices, check dimensions, select determinant/Cramer/inverse method, calculate neatly, and verify by substitution. Quadratic-check calculator This supports algebra practice used alongside matrix modelling. Module summary Represent the problem first; then choose the operation that matches the matrix structure. Trigonometry Trigonometry links angles to ratios and is used to analyse direction, slope, periodic behaviour and geometric relationships. Learning goals Classify and convert angles. Use standard trigonometric ratios. Apply Pythagorean identities and ASTC. Solve compound-angle problems. Key facts Use radians in calculus limits. ASTC determines signs by quadrant. Compound-angle formulae must preserve paired signs. Check answers with an identity or approximate value. Angles Classify acute, obtuse, right, straight, reflex, complete, positive and negative angles. The direction convention matters when an angle is measured from a reference axis. Trigonometric ratios of acute and standard angles For a right triangle, sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite/adjacent. Memorise standard values at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90° and derive reciprocal ratios when needed. Pythagorean relations, ratios of any angle, ASTC rule and reduction formula Use sin²θ+cos²θ=1, 1+tan²θ=sec²θ and 1+cot²θ=cosec²θ. The ASTC rule identifies positive ratios in quadrants I–IV: All, Sine, T

pages.title: 1003 — Engineering Graphics
pages.heading: Engineering Graphics
pages.summary: Complete Polytechnic handbook for 1003 — Engineering Graphics
pages.content: Engineering Graphics Course 1003 · Semester I · Drawing · 45 contact hours · 1.5 credits A drawing-centred handbook for accurate construction, projection, interpretation and examination practice. How the source was used The verified SITTTR syllabus text was treated as authoritative for course information, objectives, outcomes, CO–PO mapping, modules, detailed topics, instructional hours, activities, assessment, requirements, and references. How this handbook is organised Engineering graphics is the fundamental language of engineers used to communicate ideas, designs and technical information without language barriers. This handbook develops accurate construction, projection and sectioning skills. How to use this handbook 1. Learn Read the concept explanation, then restate it in your own words without changing technical terms, symbols, or units. 2. Practise Attempt the worked example and the linked activity. For drawing/CAD courses, reproduce the sequence with instruments or software. 3. Recall Close the topic, answer the module questions, and use the formula bank and revision checklist. Objectives, COs and programme mapping Official course objectives To familiarize the language of graphics used to express ideas and convey instructions while carrying out engineering jobs. To familiarize drafting and sketching skills, applications of drawing equipment and Indian Standards related to engineering drawings and dimensioning styles. To provide skills to translate ideas into sketches and draw and read engineering curves, conic sections and generation of 3D solid surfaces into plane areas. To apply basic skills to develop projection of points and lines. To familiarize the knowledge of orthographic views and sectional views of objects in engineering applications. Course outcomes CO–PO matrix Complete syllabus coverage checklist Every official major topic and detailed-syllabus entry is represented in the module sections. Use the checklist for deliberate study rather than skipping a difficult topic. Introduction This module establishes the visual grammar of engineering drawings: terminology, standards, dimensioning and regular-figure construction. Learning goals Identify instruments, sheet layouts and line types. Apply dimensioning standards. Construct four regular polygons. Key facts Use light construction lines before final outlines. Title blocks identify drawing information. Dimensions must be unambiguous. Polygon accuracy depends on equal divisions. Basic terminology of engineering graphics and standards Engineering graphics is a visual language. Learn drawing instruments, sheet sizes, board types, layout, title block, line types and the role of Indian Standards in clear technical communication. Principles of dimensioning Dimensioning communicates the size and location of features without ambiguity. Use correct extension lines, dimension lines, arrowheads, numerical values, units and spacing according to the prescribed standards. Scales are for study purpose only in this source. Choose a suitable scale when required. Place dimensions outside the object where possible. Avoid duplicated dimensions. Keep figures legible and aligned. Regular polygons Construct a pentagon, hexagon, heptagon and octagon by a suitable method when the side length is given. Begin with a clean baseline, establish the required centres or arcs, and retain construction lines lightly until verification. Module summary A neat drawing is not decoration; it is technical communication. Basic Figures Conics, miscellaneous curves and surface development extend drawing from basic figures to engineering forms. Learning goals Construct ellipse and parabola by specified methods. Draw involutes. Develop prism, cylinder and 90° elbow surfaces. Key facts Only the prescribed methods are examined. Smooth curve joining matters. Development preserves true surface lengths. The elbow is two-piece symmetric. Conic sections Study the terminology and construction of ellipse and parabola. For an ellipse use the rectangular method and concentric-circle method only. For a parabola use the tangent method only, as specified. Set the reference axes and required dimensions. Construct the control geometry. Generate points using the prescribed method. Join points with a smooth continuous curve. Miscellaneous curves Construct the involute of a circle and the involute of a rectangle. An involute is generated by unwinding a taut string from the boundary; accurate division and tangent-like arcs are important. Development of surfaces Develop the surfaces of a rectangular prism, cylinder and a 90° elbow. The elbow is a two-piece symmetric type with standard side outlets and equal cross-sectional areas. Development converts a three-dimensional surface into a plane pattern for fabrication. Module summary Method selection and construction sequence are the core skills. Basic Projections Projection theory explains how three-dimensional positions become readable two-dimensional views. Learning goals Distinguish first and third angle projection. Project points in four quadrants. Project first-quadrant lines under stated limits. Key facts XY is the reference line. Quadrant changes view positions. Projectors are perpendicular to reference planes. Keep labels and construction geometry organised. Basic projections and projection theory Outline first-angle and third-angle projection theory. Understand the reference planes and the relative placement of views before constructing projections. Projections of points Project points in all four quadrants. The location of the point relative to horizontal and vertical planes determines the relative position of its front and top views. Draw the XY reference line. Locate the point in the specified quadrant. Project perpendiculars to the reference planes. Label the front/top view consistently. Projections of lines Develop projections of lines in the first quadrant only. Questions may be limited to lines inclined to any one plane only,

pages.title: 1004 — Engineering Drawing with CAD
pages.heading: Engineering Drawing with CAD
pages.summary: Complete Polytechnic handbook for 1004 — Engineering Drawing with CAD
pages.content: Engineering Drawing with CAD Course 1004 · Semester I · Lab · 45 contact hours · 1.5 credits A practical handbook connecting manual engineering drawing, projection, sectional views and CAD workflows. How the source was used The verified SITTTR syllabus text was treated as authoritative for course information, objectives, outcomes, CO–PO mapping, modules, detailed topics, instructional hours, activities, assessment, requirements, and references. How this handbook is organised Engineering graphics is the fundamental language of engineers. This lab handbook combines manual construction, projection and CAD practice so that students can move from geometric reasoning to accurate digital drawings. How to use this handbook 1. Learn Read the concept explanation, then restate it in your own words without changing technical terms, symbols, or units. 2. Practise Attempt the worked example and the linked activity. For drawing/CAD courses, reproduce the sequence with instruments or software. 3. Recall Close the topic, answer the module questions, and use the formula bank and revision checklist. Objectives, COs and programme mapping Official course objectives To familiarize the language of graphics used to express ideas and convey instructions while carrying out engineering jobs. To provide skills to translate ideas into sketches and draw/read engineering curves, conic sections and generate 3D solid surfaces into plane areas. To apply basic skill to develop projection of points, lines, orthographic views and sectional views of objects. To familiarize the use of CAD software. To acquire skill in developing orthographic and sectional views using CAD. Course outcomes CO–PO matrix Complete syllabus coverage checklist Every official major topic and detailed-syllabus entry is represented in the module sections. Use the checklist for deliberate study rather than skipping a difficult topic. Geometrical construction and surface development Module I develops polygon, conic and surface-development skills that connect manual construction to engineering fabrication. Learning goals Construct regular polygons. Construct ellipse by two methods. Develop a prism and cylinder surface. Key facts Side length controls polygon construction. Ellipse construction must be smooth. Development preserves edges and lengths. Keep construction lines light. Drawing regular polygons Construct pentagon and hexagon by any suitable method when the side length is given. The self-learning extension includes pentagon, hexagon, heptagon and octagon terminology and construction. Set the side length and baseline. Construct the required arcs or divisions. Locate all vertices. Join and darken the final polygon. Drawing conic sections Construct an ellipse by the rectangular method and concentric-circle method. The activity also includes parabola and hyperbola construction for extended practice, while the prescribed practical experiment specifically names ellipse methods. Drawing development of surfaces Develop a rectangular prism and cylinder. The activity introduces surface-development procedures for engineering applications; measure shared edges carefully so the pattern can be folded or rolled. Module summary Construct cleanly, label method, and retain a record of the sequence. Projection, orthographic and sectional views Module II converts spatial positions and isometric figures into standard engineering views. Learning goals Use first/third-angle theory. Project points and first-quadrant lines. Create orthographic and sectional views. Key facts Quadrants determine view positions. Orthographic views must align. Minimum practical exercises are specified. Section hatching indicates cut surfaces. Drawing basic projections Outline first-angle and third-angle projection theory. Projection conventions determine where the related views are placed and must be understood before drawing. Projections of points and lines Develop projections of points in all four quadrants and projections of lines in the first quadrant only. Construct projectors accurately and keep the reference line visible until the views are checked. Draw XY reference. Locate the point or line position. Project to the relevant plane. Label and compare the resulting views. Orthographic projections and sectional views of objects Develop orthographic and sectional views of simple engineering objects from isometric figures. The practical requirement is a minimum of three orthographic exercises and two sectional exercises. Module summary Start from the reference line and maintain projection discipline. CAD software and basic commands Module III introduces the digital drafting environment and the commands needed to create, edit and annotate geometry. Learning goals Open and save drawings. Configure units, limits, grid, snap and coordinates. Use draw and modify commands. Apply properties, dimensions and text. Key facts Save often and use meaningful filenames. Object selection controls command behaviour. Line properties affect readability. Hatch is both graphical and semantic. CAD software introduction and basic commands Familiarise yourself with CAD application, advantages over manual drafting, hardware and software requirements, new/open/save/save as/exit, drawing editor, mouse and pull-down commands, help, data entry and entity selection. Drawing commands Use line, circle, arc, ellipse, rectangle, polygon, spline, polyline and hatch. Establish limits, units, grid, snap, object snap, coordinates and ortho mode before creating geometry. Modify commands, properties, dimensioning and text Practise erase, copy, array, rotate, mirror, offset, scale, move, trim, fillet, chamfer, extend, stretch, polyline edit and explode. Work with line colour, line weight, line type, dimensions and text. Module summary Build a command habit: setup, draw, modify, annotate, save. Orthographic and sectional development in CAD Module IV applies the CAD command set to complete orthographic and sectional drawing exercise

pages.summary: Complete Revision 2026 handbook for Course 1001 English for Technical Communication: LSRW skills, grammar, phonetics, translation, AI tools, professional writing, Malayalam support, practice questions and print/PDF notes.
pages.content: Handbook Navigator English for Technical Communication A complete Listening, Speaking, Reading and Writing handbook for academic, workplace and professional communication—with concise Malayalam concept support. Course at a glance Semester I Teaching Scheme 2:0:2:0 Contact Hours 60 Credits 3 CIE 40 ESE 60 Core Skills LSRW Modules 4 Purpose, outcomes and assessment identity This course connects technical knowledge with professional practice. Students learn to understand information, speak confidently, read technical and non-technical texts critically, and produce clear professional documents. Listen and identify main ideas and supporting details. Use language functions confidently in workplace and daily contexts. Read, analyse, translate and summarise varied texts. Plan, draft and produce clear technical and professional documents. Official course objectives Develop effective listening and comprehension in formal and informal contexts. Build spoken fluency and confidence for academic and workplace situations. Apply reading strategies to technical and non-technical texts. Write accurately, concisely and clearly in technical, professional and creative forms. Prerequisite and study method Prerequisite: Basic Listening, Speaking, Reading and Writing skills at Secondary Education level. Study cycle: Input → Notice language → Practise → Receive feedback → Revise → Apply in a real context. CO–PO Mapping 3 = High, 2 = Medium, 1 = Low, – = No correlation. From understanding messages to professional communication Module I Prose, comprehension, summary, word formation, sentence structure and Situational English. Module II Poetry, Tense, Active/Passive Voice, description and Reported Speech. Module III Phonetics, stress, intonation, pauses, punctuation, self-introduction, listening and notes. Module IV Translation, responsible AI use, email, letter, report and presentation. Module I — Prose 1. Listening and Reading Comprehension Original practice story: The Last Fault Before Launch On the morning a student-built solar dryer was to be demonstrated, the control display suddenly went blank. Everyone looked at the circuit board, but Meera first checked the simplest point: the emergency-stop button had been pressed during cleaning. She did not reset it immediately. She informed the instructor, isolated the supply and confirmed that no one was touching the wiring. After permission, the team reset the switch and restarted the system. The display returned, but Meera noticed an unu Comprehension check Why did Meera avoid resetting the emergency stop immediately? What evidence showed that the sensor reading was doubtful? Which qualities made Meera's response professional? State the main idea in one sentence. 2. Reading Strategies and Meaning from Context Skimming Read title, headings, first/last sentences and repeated keywords to understand the general idea. Scanning Move quickly through the text to locate a particular name, date, measurement, instruction or term. Close reading Examine argument, evidence, sequence, tone and relationships between ideas. Context clues Use definition, example, contrast and cause–effect clues to infer unfamiliar words. 3. Summarising a Passage Good summary Retains central meaning Uses concise original wording Follows logical order Excludes personal opinion unless asked Avoid Copying long phrases Adding new facts Including every example Changing the writer's meaning 4. Word Formation and Vocabulary 5. Sentence Structure, Articles and Auxiliaries Articles a before a consonant sound: a university, a motor. an before a vowel sound: an hour, an engineer. the for a specific/unique item: the main switch, the sun. Auxiliaries be, have, do form tenses, negatives and questions. Modal auxiliaries such as can, could, may, must, should express ability, permission, possibility, obligation and advice. 6. Concord / Subject–Verb Agreement 7. Situational English Request Could you please repeat the instruction? Would you mind checking this reading? Permission May I enter the laboratory? Could I use the multimeter? Clarification Do you mean that the supply must remain isolated? Could you explain the second step? Opinion and reason In my view, the test should be repeated because the readings are inconsistent. Module I — One-mark Questions 1. What is the main idea of a passage? 1 mark CO1 2. What is a supporting detail? 1 mark CO1 3. Define skimming. 1 mark CO3 4. Define scanning. 1 mark CO3 5. What is a summary? 1 mark CO4 6. Give one prefix that forms an opposite. 1 mark CO2 7. Give one suffix that forms a noun. 1 mark CO2 8. What are synonyms? 1 mark CO2 9. What are antonyms? 1 mark CO2 10. What are homonyms? 1 mark CO2 11. Name the subject in: 'The technician checks the panel.' 1 mark CO2 12. Choose the article: ___ honest engineer. 1 mark CO2 13. Choose the correct verb: Each student ___ a notebook. 1 mark CO2 14. What is an auxiliary verb? 1 mark CO2 15. Give one polite request. 1 mark CO2 Module I — Three-mark Questions 1. Differentiate skimming and scanning. 3 marks CO1 2. Write three rules for an effective summary. 3 marks CO4 3. Explain prefix, suffix and root with one example each. 3 marks CO2 4. State three rules of subject–verb agreement. 3 marks CO2 5. Explain the use of a, an and the. 3 marks CO2 6. Write a short workplace conversation requesting permission. 3 marks CO2 7. Identify the sentence pattern: 'The manager gave the trainee a task.' 3 marks CO2 8. Explain how context clues help vocabulary learning. 3 marks CO3 9. Write three expressions for stating an opinion politely. 3 marks CO2 10. Write three qualities of effective situational English. 3 marks CO2 Module I — Seven-mark Questions 1. Read an unfamiliar technical passage and explain a complete comprehension strategy. 7 marks CO1 2. Summarise the original practice story in 80–100 words. 7 marks CO4 3. Explain sentence structure, articles, auxiliaries and concord with examples. 7 marks CO2 4. Prepare a real-life conversation betwe

pages.title: Course 1002 — Fundamentals of Engineering Mathematics | REV2026 | POLY PMNA
pages.heading: Fundamentals of Engineering Mathematics
pages.summary: Complete Kerala Diploma Revision 2026 handbook for Course 1002 Fundamentals of Engineering Mathematics: syllabus coverage, Malayalam support, diagrams, questions and printable notes.
pages.content: POLY PMNA · Diploma Curriculum Revision 2026 Fundamentals of Engineering Mathematics A complete syllabus-aligned handbook with clear explanations, practical or exam guidance, Malayalam-support notes, diagrams, activities and revision tools. Programmes Diploma in Engineering and Technology Contact hours 60 Teaching scheme 3:1:0:0 Credits 4 CIE / ESE Theory CIE 40 / Theory ESE 60 Self-learning 5.5 h/week; 60 h total Curriculum integrity Official Source Declaration and Verified Inconsistencies This handbook is based only on the supplied official Diploma Curriculum Revision 2026 syllabus PDF for Course 1002 , titled Fundamentals of Engineering Mathematics . Objectives, course outcomes, teaching scheme, major topics, detailed coverage, activities and assessment are drawn from that source. Course dashboard What You Are Expected to Learn Course introduction This foundation course develops mathematical tools used in engineering: matrices, trigonometry, coordinate geometry and differential calculus. The emphasis is on accurate symbolic work, clear diagrams and a reproducible problem-solving method. Prerequisite foundation Linear equations, quadratic equations, rectangular coordinates and angles from Secondary Education. Use prerequisites only as a revision bridge. The current course outcomes and detailed syllabus define the required performance. Study method How to Use This Handbook 1 · Understand Read terms, conditions and purpose; make a short definition in your own words. 2 · Visualise Follow the diagram, circuit, flow or procedure and label it accurately. 3 · Apply Use the method block, calculation or practical checklist without skipping units or safety checks. 4 · Revise Use questions, quick cards and common-mistake notes before examination. Official statements Objectives and Course Outcomes Official course objectives Apply matrices and determinants to linear equations. Use trigonometric concepts and relationships. Represent and interpret straight lines and circles. Evaluate limits and derivatives. Student-friendly meaning You should be able to recognise the relevant system or material, explain its principle, communicate through a correct diagram/table where needed and follow a defensible solution or practical method. Syllabus coverage Curriculum Coverage Map Learning roadmap How the Modules Connect Matrices and Determinants Matrix concept and types; transpose; algebra; determinants; minors/cofactors; adjoint/inverse of 2×2 matrix; Cramer’s rule. CO1 · 11 L + 4 T hours Trigonometry Angles; ratios; standard angles; Pythagorean relations; ASTC and reduction; compound angles. CO2 · 11 L + 4 T hours Coordinate Geometry Slope and slope-point line; angle between lines; parallel/perpendicular lines; circle equation, centre and radius. CO3 · 11 L + 4 T hours Differential Calculus Limits by substitution/factorisation; special forms; derivative concept and standard results; rules and second derivatives. CO4 · 12 L + 3 T hours Module 1 Matrices and Determinants Matrix concept and types; transpose; algebra; determinants; minors/cofactors; adjoint/inverse of 2×2 matrix; Cramer’s rule. Learning goals Identify core terms, explain the principle and complete the stated application or practical outcome. Key evidence Use a labelled diagram, table, graph, procedure or calculation that matches the topic. Engineering habit Check units, polarity/direction, ratings, materials and safety before concluding. 1. Matrices, order and special types A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of entries. Its order is rows by columns. The official types include row, column, square, diagonal, triangular, identity and zero matrices. Type and order determine which operations are meaningful. Study and application method Write order first, identify the requested type by checking positions of entries, and preserve brackets when presenting a matrix. Connect the explanation to the official student learning outcome before attempting a numerical, diagram, procedure or viva answer. Evidence of understanding Use correct terminology, a labelled sketch/table where useful, correct units or conditions, and a conclusion linked to the observed or calculated result. How to construct a complete answer Given: identify the quantities, device condition, waveform or circuit arrangement. Required: state exactly what must be found or explained. Method: Write order first, identify the requested type by checking positions of entries, and preserve brackets when presenting a matrix. Answer habit: show a labelled step, the relevant unit/condition and a short interpretation. 2. Transpose and algebra of matrices Transpose interchanges rows and columns. Matrix algebra includes scalar multiplication, equality, addition, subtraction and multiplication. Matrix multiplication is an ordered row-by-column operation and is generally not commutative. Study and application method For multiplication, check inner dimensions, compute each entry as row-dot-column and state final order. Connect the explanation to the official student learning outcome before attempting a numerical, diagram, procedure or viva answer. Evidence of understanding Use correct terminology, a labelled sketch/table where useful, correct units or conditions, and a conclusion linked to the observed or calculated result. How to construct a complete answer Given: identify the quantities, device condition, waveform or circuit arrangement. Required: state exactly what must be found or explained. Method: For multiplication, check inner dimensions, compute each entry as row-dot-column and state final order. Answer habit: show a labelled step, the relevant unit/condition and a short interpretation. 3. Determinants, inverse and Cramer’s rule A determinant is associated with a square matrix. Minors and cofactors support adjoint construction; a 2×2 inverse exists when determinant is nonzero. Cramer’s rule solves a compatible linear system through determinant ratios. pages.content: Engineering Drawing with CAD Course Code 1004 — Complete Polytechnic Revision 2026 Handbook Programme(s) AI, AI & ML, Biomedical Engg, Cloud & Big Data, Cyber Forensics, CS & Tech, CS & Engg, Computer Engg, CS & Engg (AI & ML), Electronics & Comm, Electronics Engg, Electronics Engg (Embedded Systems), Electronics & Computer Engg, IC Design & Fabrication, Instrumentation Engg, IT, Micro Electronics, Automation & Robotics, RPA, Textile Tech Subject Code 1004 Semester I Course Type Lab Teaching Scheme (L:T:P:R) 0:0:3:0 Contact Hours 45 Credits 1.5 CIE Marks 60 ESE Marks 40 Official Source Declaration Course Dashboard Course Introduction Engineering graphics is the fundamental language of engineers used to visually communicate ideas, designs, and technical information without any language barriers. Its objectives include developing the ability to interpret and create accurate drawings. Understanding the shape, size, and relationship of components, and applying standards for clear communication. It also enhances spatial visualization and supports the effective planning and manufacture of engineering products. Introduction of CAD Pre-requisites Basic Geometry (Secondary Education) L: Lecture (1 credit), T: Tutorial (1 credit), P: Practical (0.5 credit), S: Project (0.5 credit), SS: Self-Learning, CIE: Continuous Internal Evaluation, ESE: End Semester Examination How to Use This Handbook Course Outcomes & CO–PO Mapping Course Objectives To familiarize the language of graphics which is used to express ideas, convey instructions while carrying out engineering jobs. Provide skills to translate ideas into sketches and to draw and read various engineering curves, conic sections and the generation of 3D solid surfaces into plane areas. To apply basic skill to develop projection of points, lines, orthographic views and sectional views of objects. To familiarize the use of CAD software. To acquire skill in developing orthographic and sectional views using CAD. Course Outcomes (CO) CO–PO Mapping Curriculum Coverage Map How the Modules Connect Modules I & II build manual drawing skills; Modules III & IV transfer those skills to CAD software, ending with digital orthographic and sectional views. Drawing — Regular Polygons, Conic Sections & Development of Surfaces Learn to construct regular polygons, draw conic sections (ellipse, parabola, hyperbola), and develop surfaces of 3D solids into 2D patterns. 1.1 Regular Polygons — Construction of Pentagon & Hexagon Definition: A regular polygon is a closed plane figure with all sides equal in length and all interior angles equal. Common regular polygons used in engineering drawing include pentagon (5 sides), hexagon (6 sides), heptagon (7 sides), and octagon (8 sides). Key Terminology: Side (s): Length of each equal side. Interior angle: (n − 2) × 180° / n where n is the number of sides. Exterior angle: 360° / n Circumradius (R): Radius of the circle passing through all vertices. Apothem (r): Distance from centre to midpoint of a side. Construction of a Regular Pentagon (Side Length Given) Method: General method using circumcircle Calculate the circumradius using R = s / (2 × sin(36°)). Draw a circle with radius R and mark the centre O. Draw a vertical diameter AB. Divide the circle into 5 equal parts (72° each) using a protractor or compass. Join the consecutive points to form the pentagon. Given: Side length = 40 mm. Construct a regular pentagon. R = 40 / (2 × sin 36°) = 40 / (2 × 0.5878) = 40 / 1.1756 ≈ 34.03 mm. Draw circle of radius 34.03 mm, divide into 5 equal parts (72°), join the points. Construction of a Regular Hexagon (Side Length Given) Method: Using circumcircle Calculate R = s (since sin 30° = 0.5, R = s / (2 × 0.5) = s). Draw a circle with radius equal to the given side length. Mark any point on the circle as the first vertex. Using the same radius, step off 6 equal divisions around the circle (60° each). Join the points to get the hexagon. Given: Side length = 30 mm. Construct a regular hexagon. Since R = s = 30 mm, draw a circle of radius 30 mm. Step off 6 divisions of 30 mm along the circumference. Join the points. 1.2 Conic Sections — Ellipse (Rectangular & Concentric Circle Methods) Definition: Conic sections are curves obtained by intersecting a right circular cone with a plane. The three main conic sections are: Ellipse: Plane cuts all generators of the cone (angle between plane and axis > semi-vertical angle). Parabola: Plane is parallel to one generator (angle = semi-vertical angle). Hyperbola: Plane cuts both nappes (angle < semi-vertical angle). Ellipse — Rectangular Method This method is used when the major and minor axes are given. Draw the major axis AB and minor axis CD intersecting at O. Construct a rectangle with sides equal to AB and CD. Divide the rectangle into equal parts horizontally and vertically. Draw lines from the ends of the axes through the division points. Mark the intersections and draw a smooth curve through them. Ellipse — Concentric Circle Method This method uses two concentric circles with diameters equal to the major and minor axes. Draw two concentric circles with diameters equal to the major axis (outer) and minor axis (inner). Divide the circles into 12 equal parts (30° intervals). From each division on the outer circle, draw a vertical line downward. From each division on the inner circle, draw a horizontal line outward. The intersections of these lines give points on the ellipse. Join the points with a smooth curve. Given: Major axis = 80 mm, Minor axis = 50 mm. Draw circles of radii 40 mm and 25 mm. Divide into 12 parts. Project vertically from outer circle and horizontally from inner circle. Intersection points trace the ellipse. 1.3 Development of Surfaces — Rectangular Prism & Cylinder Definition: Development of a surface is the process of unfolding a 3D solid's surface into a 2D plane (a net). It is used in sheet metal work, packaging, and fabrication to determine the exact shape and size of material

CO2: Practice appropriate masonry and finishing techniques for durable and quality building construction. Curriculum Coverage Map Learning roadmap Fundamentals of Civil Engineering Civil engineering converts social needs into safe, serviceable and durable infrastructure. This module begins with the profession, then moves to building classification, site selection, regulatory area terms and basic surveying. 1. Relevance and major disciplines Civil engineering supports shelter, transportation, water supply, sanitation, irrigation, energy infrastructure and environmental protection. Major disciplines include structural, geotechnical, transportation, water resources, environmental, construction management and surveying/geomatics. 2. Buildings by occupancy and construction type Occupancy classification groups buildings according to their principal use. Typical NBC groups include residential, educational, institutional, assembly, business, mercantile, industrial, storage and hazardous. Always verify the current approved NBC/Kerala rule classification before statutory submission. Load-bearing structure Walls carry floor and roof loads to the foundation. Suitable for limited spans and low-rise construction. Openings and later alterations require care. Framed structure Beams and columns carry loads; walls mainly enclose spaces. Offers larger openings and flexible planning but needs engineered detailing. 3. Site selection Confirm legal title, access and permitted land use. Study ground slope, drainage, flood risk and soil condition. Check water, electricity, road, sewer/septic feasibility and emergency access. Consider orientation, ventilation, sunlight, noise and future expansion. Avoid unstable slopes, filled lowland and uncontrolled watercourses unless engineered mitigation is approved. 4. Building area concepts, Coverage and FSI Covered built-up area measured at floor level, generally including wall thickness according to the applicable measurement rule. Total constructed floor area; exact inclusions must follow the applicable authority's definitions. Usable covered area measured within the building after prescribed exclusions. Net usable area where a carpet can be laid, excluding wall thickness and specified service/common areas. Solved example Given: Plot = 300 m², ground coverage = 120 m², total floor area = 240 m². Coverage = 120/300 × 100 = 40% . FSI = 240/300 = 0.80 . These calculations do not prove statutory compliance; compare with the current Kerala Building Rules and sanctioning authority limits. 5. Two basic principles are: work from whole to part, and fix a point by at least two independent measurements. Common units: millimetre, metre, kilometre; square metre, hectare; degree-minute-second or decimal degree. Course overview What this handbook covers The structure follows the supplied official SITTTR Kerala Revision 2026 syllabus. It is a learning handbook rather than a replacement for the official syllabus PDF. Use the module checklist to ensure that every prescribed point has been revised. Apply fundamental electrical quantities, Ohm’s law, resistor combinations and division rules. Interpret AC parameters, electrical safety devices and power in single-phase circuits. Identify, test and apply resistors, capacitors and inductors using appropriate instruments. Explain and demonstrate semiconductor devices, half-wave rectification, transistors and logic gates. Module roadmap Visual concept See the subject as a system Module I Electrical fundamentals, resistor networks and measurement Electrical quantities and units Define charge, current, voltage, resistance, power and energy. Use A, V, Ω, W, J, Wh and kWh correctly and distinguish power from energy. Ohm’s law For a conductor at constant physical conditions, V = IR. Solve for any unknown and check whether the assumed linear relationship is valid. Series resistance Same current flows through every resistor; equivalent resistance is the sum. Voltage divides in proportion to resistance. Parallel resistance Same voltage appears across branches; branch currents add. Equivalent resistance is less than the smallest branch resistance. Voltage and current division Use Vx = Vs Rx/ΣR for series networks and branch-current relations for parallel networks. Confirm results with KVL/KCL. Symbols and instruments Identify source, switch, resistor, lamp, fuse, earth, ammeter, voltmeter, wattmeter and rheostat symbols. Select instrument, function, AC/DC mode and range. DC voltage/current measurement Connect a voltmeter across the element and an ammeter in series. Apply the correct multiplication factor on a multirange instrument. Rules / common mistakes De-energise before changing wiring. Start with the highest meter range. Never place an ammeter directly across a source. Check polarity for DC measurements. Practice and self-learning Identify basic circuit symbols and measuring instruments. Use tester and multimeter safely. Build a DC resistor circuit and measure voltage/current; compare with calculation. Module II AC parameters, electrical safety and AC power Sinusoidal terms Define cycle, frequency, time period, angular frequency, amplitude, instantaneous value, maximum value, RMS value, average value, form factor and peak factor. Instantaneous equation Write v = Vm sin(ωt + φ), where ω = 2πf. Relate frequency and period by T = 1/f. RMS and average values For a sine wave Vrms = Vm/√2, Vavg over a half-cycle = 2Vm/π, form factor ≈ 1.11 and peak factor = √2. Electrical safety precautions Isolation, earthing, dry hands, rated tools, lockout/tagout where applicable, correct PPE, one-hand technique for live diagnostics and immediate first-aid response. Fuse, MCB, MCCB, ELCB and RCCB Explain operating purpose, rating and limitation. A fuse/MCB responds to overcurrent; RCCB responds to residual current and does not replace overcurrent protection. AC power Define active P = VI cosφ, reactive Q = VI sinφ and apparent S = VI. Explain power factor and the power triangle. Measurement of AC parameters Construct a simple source–switch–fuse–load circuit and measure voltage, current and power using correctly rated instruments. Rules / common mistakes Treat every conductor as live until proved dead. RCCB test button should be checked periodically. Do not bypass a protective device. Use instrument category and voltage rating appropriate to the installation. Practice and self-learning Identify safety devices in a residential distribution board. Sketch a 230 V, 50 Hz waveform and calculate peak/time period. Measure voltage, current and power of a safe laboratory AC load. Module III Passive components, breadboard, DSO and measurement Resistors Fixed carbon composition and wire-wound resistors; variable potentiometer, rheostat and trimmer. Select resistance, tolerance and power rating. Four-band colour code First two bands are significant digits, third is multiplier and fourth is tolerance. Verify decoded value with a digital multimeter. Inductance Define inductance, self-inductance and mutual inductance, measured in henry. Explain energy storage in magnetic field and common applications. Capacitance Define capacitance, fixed and variable capacitor types, polarity and voltage rating. Use series and parallel combination equations. Breadboard construction Recognise power rails and connected terminal groups. Build a 3 V LED circuit from a 5 V source using a current-limiting resistor and switch. DSO operation Identify vertical/horizontal controls, select 1×/10× probe, compensate probe with calibration output, set trigger and compute Vmax, Vpp and period. LCR measurement Identify capacitor types/codes, measure capacitance and inductance, and construct a simple wound inductor on a toroidal or EE core without design calculation.
